metadata.title: Predicting science achievement scores with machine learning algorithms: a case study of OECD PISA 2015–2018 data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA 2015 microdata for 13 countries and predicts PISA 2018 science outcomes using supervised machine learning. Although PISA is collected under a complex sampling design, the manuscript does not report applying any student/sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures in the ML training/testing pipeline. The authors instead describe a country-wise random training/test split (75%/25%) and hyperparameter tuning via grid search with 10-fold cross-validation, implying standard ML estimation without survey-weight adjustments. Because tree-based ML methods (XGBoost, Random Forest, SVR) are not natively weight-aware in the way IEA/OECD scaling software is, the absence of explicit weighting suggests an unweighted analysis; results should therefore be interpreted as predictive associations rather than population-representative estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses OECD PISA 2015 science literacy data for 13 randomly selected countries (Brazil, Chinese Taipei, Dominican Republic, Estonia, Finland, Hungary, Italy, Japan, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Peru, Singapore, Türkiye). It restricts the analysis to these countries only (not the full 72-country PISA 2015 population) and uses PV2SCIE as the science achievement outcome. For each country, the PISA-2015 data are randomly split into training and testing sets (75% training, 25% testing) to evaluate model performance. Missing values detected in a small number of cases are excluded during preprocessing (complete-case style), and the same set of 18 predictor variables is used as inputs for predicting PISA 2018 science outcomes.

main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost (best): by-country testing r ranges ~0.442–0.678; Luxembourg testing r=0.678, RMSE=70.83, MAE=57.06; Finland testing r=0.538, RMSE=75.97, MAE=59.90. Overall: moderate correlations (0.40<r<0.69).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science (PV2SCIE) data for 13 countries, the study leveraged science learning time (SMINS), socioeconomic status (ESCS), home possessions (HOMEPOS), and total learning time (TMINS) to predict students’ PISA-2015 science achievement, finding that XGBoost achieved the highest predictive performance across all countries. This indicates that non-linear ensemble models can more accurately capture how learning time and socioeconomic resources relate to science achievement than linear regression, suggesting that education systems may benefit from data-driven targeting of time-on-science and resource supports rather than relying on simple linear relationships.

main_findings.target_variable: PISA 2018 science achievement (PV2SCIE) predicted from PISA 2015
main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost (best): Luxembourg r=0.600, RMSE=75.06, MAE=59.97; Finland r=0.467, RMSE=79.38, MAE=63.24. Across countries: moderate correlations (0.40<r<0.69). Table 5/6 show XGBoost outperforming MLR/SVR/RF for each country; MLR lowest by-country.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science data to predict PISA 2018 science achievement (PV2SCIE) for students in 13 countries, the study leveraged SMINS, ESCS, HOMEPOS, and TMINS to forecast future science performance, finding that XGBoost produced the best transfer performance with moderate correlations between predicted and actual scores (0.40<r<0.69). This indicates that strengthening science learning time and addressing socioeconomic disparities may improve future science outcomes, though the study’s predictive design does not establish causal effects and performance is weaker at extreme achievement values.

main_findings.target_variable: Country average science achievement (PISA 2018) predicted from PISA 2015
main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost (best): country mean PV2SCIE estimates closely match observed means; e.g., Luxembourg observed 501±93 vs XGBoost predicted 501±62; Finland observed 536±89 vs XGBoost predicted 536±49. Two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test: no significant distribution difference between predicted and actual PISA-2018 science scores (p>0.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science predictors to estimate PISA 2018 country-average science achievement for the same 13 countries, the study leveraged SMINS, ESCS, HOMEPOS, and TMINS to predict aggregated outcomes, finding that XGBoost estimated country mean science scores with very high accuracy and produced predicted distributions statistically similar to observed ones (KS test p>0.05). This indicates that policymakers can use ML-based forecasting to monitor likely shifts in national science performance and to prioritize interventions aligned with learning-time and socioeconomic gradients, while recognizing that the approach is correlational and may underperform for countries/students at the extremes.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses OECD PISA 2015 science literacy data (PV2SCIE) from 13 randomly selected countries (N=67,329) and predicts both (i) students’ PISA-2015 science scores and (ii) students’ PISA-2018 science scores using the same 18 predictors. For each country, the authors split PISA-2015 data into training (75%) and testing (25%) sets, tune hyperparameters via grid search with 10-fold cross-validation, and evaluate models using Pearson’s r, RMSE, and MAE. Across all countries, XGBoost consistently outperformed MLR, SVR, and Random Forest; for PISA-2018, Luxembourg achieved the highest predictive correlation (r=0.600, RMSE=75.06, MAE=59.97) and Finland the lowest (r=0.467, RMSE=79.38, MAE=63.24), with correlations generally in the moderate range (0.40<r<0.69). Missing values were excluded during preprocessing, and the manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights, so results should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than population-representative causal effects. The authors also note reduced accuracy at extreme achievement values.
